summary: Steven Moon, founder of Hai, advocates deploying enterprise AI agents within existing security boundaries rather than building parallel systems. He frames the current moment as historically unique: LLMs enable software that understands humans directly and can use the same interfaces people do. Yet engineers keep building new AI portals, dashboards, credentials, and security reviews—recreating the obsolete SaaS pattern. Moon cites Satya Nadella's observation that "SaaS is dead," signaling AI agents becoming the primary interaction layer for business software. Moon argues AI agents should behave like any other employee: following security policies, using approved systems, staying within data boundaries, accessing only what is needed, and being monitored and audited. Enterprises already have everything required—secure compute environments, identity management, data governance, compliance frameworks, audit capabilities, and private clouds—refined over decades. At Hai, building on Microsoft 365 and their ecosystem means inheriting battle-tested trust and infrastructure. Jensen Huang's observation that "the IT department of every company is going to be the HR department of AI agents" captures the provisioning model: IT creates agent accounts in Active Directory, applies standard policies, sets permissions, and uses existing audit tools—no new systems to learn. Moon highlights email as a powerful pattern for agent-to-agent communication: fully logged, auditable, permission-enforced through existing systems, and transparent. The same patterns work with Google Workspace or other enterprise platforms. The core insight is leveraging existing infrastructure—identity management, security controls, compliance frameworks, enterprise-grade APIs—rather than reinventing it. The future of enterprise AI is enhancing systems perfected over decades, not building new interfaces. Document management, internal messaging, and workflow tools become potential gateways for AI capabilities. The era of mandatory translation layers between humans and machines is ending; the era of direct understanding and seamless AI collaboration has begun.

takeaways: AI agents should operate within existing enterprise security boundaries, following the same policies, systems, and audit controls as human employees.
Enterprises already possess the necessary infrastructure—private clouds, identity management, data governance, compliance frameworks—so no parallel systems need to be built.
Traditional SaaS interfaces are becoming obsolete; AI agents are becoming the primary way to interact with business systems.
IT departments can provision and manage AI agents exactly like human employees using existing Active Directory, security policies, permissions, and audit tools.
Email provides a powerful, fully logged and auditable pattern for agent-to-agent communication at enterprise scale.
Building on platforms like Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace inherits years of hardened security and compliance into AI agents.
Engineers should enhance existing trusted systems with AI capabilities rather than building new portals, dashboards, or translation layers.
The era of mandatory translation layers between humans and machines is ending, replaced by direct understanding and seamless AI collaboration.

sections.title: Introduction: AI Agents Within Existing Security Boundaries
sections.summary: Steven Moon introduces himself as founder of Hai, building enterprise AI agents that operate entirely within existing security boundaries. He frames the challenge as deploying digital workers that respect enterprise security, compliance, and workflows rather than just building powerful models.

sections.title: A New Computing Paradigm and the Obsolescence of SaaS
sections.summary: Moon describes LLMs as a new paradigm where software understands humans directly and can use the same interfaces as people. Yet engineers keep building new portals, dashboards, and credentials. He cites Satya Nadella's observation that 'SaaS is dead,' signaling AI agents becoming the primary interface for business systems, making traditional SaaS patterns obsolete.

sections.title: AI Agents Should Work Like Human Employees
sections.summary: Enterprises already have everything needed—secure compute, identity management, data governance, compliance, audit capabilities, and private clouds—refined over decades. Moon argues AI agents should follow security policies, use approved systems, stay within data boundaries, and be monitored like any employee. Modern infrastructure lets agents run in private clouds with full oversight.

sections.title: IT Departments Become HR for AI Agents
sections.summary: Citing Jensen Huang's statement that IT will become the HR department for AI agents, Moon explains that IT can create agent accounts in Active Directory, apply standard security policies, set permissions through familiar interfaces, and use existing audit and monitoring tools—no new systems required, just another employee to manage.

sections.title: Email as Agent-to-Agent Communication Pattern
sections.summary: Moon highlights email as a powerful pattern for agent-to-agent communication: every interaction is logged, auditable, permission-enforced through existing systems, and data flows are transparent. While Hai chose Microsoft's ecosystem, the same patterns work with Google Workspace or other enterprise platforms, all offering built-in identity, security, compliance, and APIs.

sections.title: Enhancing Existing Systems and the End of Translation Layers
sections.summary: The future of enterprise AI is enhancing systems perfected over decades, not building new interfaces. Document management, internal messaging, and workflow tools become potential gateways for AI. Moon argues engineers should ask which existing systems can be enhanced rather than what new tools to build. The era of mandatory translation layers is ending; the era of direct understanding and seamless AI collaboration has begun.
